title: What the experience curve does not explain
bodyMd:
For half a century, manufacturers and the governments that subsidise them have relied on a striking empirical regularity: the unit cost of a manufactured good tends to fall by a roughly constant percentage each time cumulative output doubles. The relationship, usually called the experience curve, has been documented for airframes, semiconductors, photovoltaic modules and battery cells, and it is unusually stable across industries that otherwise have little in common. Its policy appeal is obvious. If cost falls as accumulated production grows, then a government that buys enough of an expensive new technology early is not merely purchasing hardware; it is purchasing a permanently lower price for everyone who buys later.

The regularity is real. The causal reading attached to it is not secure, for two reasons. The first is confounding. Cumulative output is an unusually poor explanatory variable because almost everything else moves alongside it: as cumulative output grows, so do annual production volume, plant size, the maturity of the product design and, frequently, the scale of the industries supplying raw materials. The few studies that hold these apart — comparing plants of identical scale building an unchanged design — find that learning by doing is genuine but accounts for a minority of the observed decline. The second reason is selection. Experience curves are estimated for technologies that reached high cumulative volumes, which is to say for the ones that succeeded. Technologies whose costs stayed stubbornly high never accumulated the output needed to enter the sample at all, so a curve that describes survivors is routinely read as though it described all entrants.

None of this shows that subsidy is futile. It shows that the mechanism determines the instrument. If falling costs come chiefly from plant scale, the effective policy aggregates demand so that larger plants can be financed. If they come from cheaper inputs, the leverage lies upstream, in the materials industries, and not in the finished product at all. And if genuine learning dominates, subsidy should follow production experience within individual firms and should be withdrawn as that experience accumulates. Telling the three apart requires plant-level cost data that firms rarely release — which is the unglamorous reason the single curve, whatever its weaknesses, remains in use.
accessibilityText: A three-paragraph prose passage about the experience curve in manufacturing. The first paragraph describes the empirical regularity that unit cost falls by a roughly constant percentage each time cumulative output doubles, and explains why this makes early government purchasing look like an investment in permanently lower prices. The second paragraph grants that the regularity is real but attacks the causal reading on two grounds: confounding, since plant size, annual volume, design maturity and supplier scale all move with cumulative output, and studies holding these constant find learning by doing explains only a minority of the decline; and selection, since curves are estimated only for technologies that reached high volumes, so a curve describing survivors is read as though it described all entrants. The third paragraph says subsidy is not futile but that the mechanism should determine the instrument, listing three different policy responses depending on whether scale, input prices or learning dominates, and notes that telling them apart needs plant-level cost data firms rarely release.
